article.title: 55/45 is a really close race
article.subtitle: Life lessons from gambling about understanding election probabilities.

extraction.summary: Silver argues that a 55/45 Electoral College forecast is essentially a toss-up and should not be read as a vote-share prediction. He draws on sports betting and poker to explain how to interpret small probabilistic edges. He then explains why the 2024 Silver Bulletin model's win probabilities swing a lot while its popular-vote forecast barely moves: when a race is late and close, the translation from popular vote to Electoral College is steep, much like win-probability curves in a close NBA or MLB game. A chart table shows Harris win probability by popular-vote margin, revealing a sizeable Electoral College bias toward Trump. The article also touches on the model's convention bounce adjustment, simulation averages since the July 30 relaunch, few undecided voters, and the limits of poll accuracy.

findings.statement: A 55/45 Electoral College win probability from the Silver Bulletin model means the favored candidate wins about 11 times out of 20. It is not a vote-share forecast and is essentially a toss-up for most practical purposes.
findings.rationale: People confuse win probability with vote share. A 55-45 vote share would be the biggest landslide since Reagan in 1984.
findings.evidence_quote: even though this isn't any different from 50/50 for most practical purposes

findings.statement: Silver suggests framing probabilities as odds ratios. A 3:1 advantage is meaningful in a way that 11:9 (a 55/45 split) is not.
findings.evidence_quote: Framing probabilities in odds ratios like this can sometimes be helpful. A 3:1 advantage is meaningful in the way that 11:9 just isn't.

findings.statement: Averaged over all forecasts since the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model relaunched on July 30, 2024, Harris won 49.4% of simulations and Trump 50.2%. The remainder reflects 269-269 Electoral College ties, which the model simulates as a separate outcome.
findings.evidence_quote: Harris has won 49.4 percent of simulations, and Trump has won 50.2 percent. (These don't quite add up to 100 because of the slim possibility of a 269-269 Electoral College tie.)

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model includes a convention bounce adjustment that discounts a party's polls after its convention. Its effects lingered after the DNC and helped push the forecast toward Trump in late August and early September 2024.
findings.rationale: Post-convention periods are typically among a candidate's best polling periods, so the polls are discounted.
findings.evidence_quote: the lingering effects of the model's convention bounce adjustment

findings.statement: The weeks right after a party's convention are typically among the best polling periods for that party's candidate. Harris was atypical in 2024 because her polls declined after the DNC.
findings.evidence_quote: her polls began declining after her convention when typically this is one of the best periods of polling for a candidate

findings.statement: Economic data feed into the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential forecast. Economic headwinds in late August and early September 2024 contributed to the forecast drifting toward Trump, and later data were better.
findings.evidence_quote: plus some economic headwinds (there's since been better data)

findings.statement: Shifts in a series of high-quality national polls carried significant weight in moving the Silver Bulletin 2024 forecast. This implies that polls are weighted by quality.
findings.evidence_quote: shifts against Harris in a series of high-quality national polls

findings.statement: In the Silver Bulletin 2024 model, the mapping from national popular-vote margin to Electoral College win probability is steep around the tipping region. Moving from a 2-3 point Harris popular-vote lead to a 3-4 point lead raises her win probability from about 28% to 59% (the chart table gives 58.8%). So small popular-vote changes produce large probability swings.

quantities.name: Harris win prob at D+1 to +2 (text: '2-point lead rounded down')
Harris win prob at D+2 to +3

findings.rationale: It is analogous to late-and-close win probability curves in sports.
findings.evidence_quote: If she goes from a 2-point popular vote lead (rounded down) to a 3-point lead, Harris's win probability zooms up from 28 percent to 59 percent.

findings.rationale: Shows the conditional EC outcome distribution across simulations.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 model reports win probabilities that may not add to 100% because in some simulations neither candidate wins a majority of electoral votes.

The Silver Bulletin 2024 popular-vote forecast barely moved from model launch to Oct 7, 2024, apart from a jump when RFK Jr. dropped out and both candidates gained. The Electoral College probability, by contrast, swung between roughly 35% and 64% for Harris, because of the steep popular-vote-to-EC mapping.
findings.evidence_quote: Our forecast of the popular vote has barely moved, other than when RFK Jr. quit the race and both candidates gained ground

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 model forecast RFK Jr.'s popular vote at roughly 3-4% until he dropped out in late August. After his exit, both Harris and Trump's projected vote shares jumped (about 49 to 50.5 for Harris and 46.5 to 48 for Trump in the chart), meaning his support was reallocated to both.
The Silver Bulletin 2024 popular-vote forecast chart displays 80% intervals for each candidate's vote share. On Oct 7, the band ran roughly ±2.5 points around each candidate's projection.

Polls are not accurate enough to support much more than 50/50 to 60/40 confidence in a race this close. Unlike a sports final score, the final polling average before Election Day isn't always correct.
findings.evidence_quote: polls simply aren't accurate enough to provide for much more confidence than that

findings.statement: With four weeks left, Silver expects the 2024 probabilities to stay in the 50/50 to 60/40 range. His reason is that there are extremely few undecided voters: Harris plus Trump total 95.5% in the Silver Bulletin national average, and third parties typically take another 1-2%.
findings.rationale: Not enough votes are in play to move the needle.
findings.evidence_quote: there just aren't enough votes in play to really move the needle

findings.statement: If your model says 55/45 and prediction markets say the reverse, you have a profitable wager, but you will still lose almost half the time. Silver notes there have been much bigger model-market discrepancies in the past. At the time, Polymarket had Trump about 53.7% and Harris 45.6%.
findings.evidence_quote: you have a profitable wager — but you're still going to lose the bet almost half the time

findings.statement: Experienced sports bettors avoid marginal edges such as 53/47 or 54/46, just above the 52.5% vig breakeven. They do this to reduce variance and because there is ultimately no way to know their model is right. Silver's point is that small model edges deserve humility.
findings.evidence_quote: there's ultimately no way to know that your model is right

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential forecast relaunched on July 30, 2024, after Harris replaced Biden.
findings.evidence_quote: since our forecast relaunch on July 30

findings.statement: In the weeks before the Sept 10, 2024 debate, the Silver Bulletin model implicitly hypothesized that momentum was shifting against Harris. Silver notes this hypothesis cannot be properly tested because the debate intervened.
findings.evidence_quote: The model's hypothesis that the momentum had been shifting against Harris before the debate will never quite be appropriately tested

political_insights.insight: In 2024, Democrats needed roughly a 2.5-point national popular-vote lead to be favored in the Electoral College. A Harris popular-vote win of 0-1 points gave her only about a 9.5% chance.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model the popular vote and the EC separately. The EC gap is sizeable and asymmetric.

political_insights.insight: Harris won the Sept 2024 debate and reestablished a consistent lead of about 3 points in national polls.
political_insights.evidence: Forecast chart shift after the Sept 10 debate

political_insights.insight: RFK Jr.'s exit raised both major candidates' vote shares.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Reallocate a dropping-out third-party candidate's support to both major candidates, not just one.

political_insights.insight: In 2024, very few voters were undecided: the major candidates combined for 95.5% and third parties typically get 1-2%. This limits late movement.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Late-race volatility should be lower when the undecided share is small.

references.description: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential forecast and methodology (convention bounce adjustment)
Greg Stoll MLB win probability data

open_questions: Functional form and duration of the convention bounce adjustment.
How economic indicators enter the 2024 model and their weight.
Number of simulations run per forecast update.
How RFK Jr.'s support was reallocated between Harris and Trump upon his exit.
Size and distribution of the assumed national polling error behind the steep popular-vote-to-EC mapping.
